title: How LLMs Are Trained
brief: This quiz covers the pipeline that turns a raw text predictor into a helpful assistant: pretraining on next-token prediction, instruction tuning, and preference tuning with RLHF or DPO. Understanding these stages explains why modern chatbots behave the way they do.

questions.question: What objective are GPT-style language models pretrained on, before any fine-tuning happens?
questions.answer: They are pretrained to predict the next word, or token, in a sequence of text across a vast corpus.
key_points: Done on a vast amount of text
questions.hint: Think about what the model guesses at every position in a sentence.
questions.fun_fact: GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer, and the name literally describes this pretraining step.

questions.question: After pretraining, what is instruction tuning meant to accomplish?
questions.answer: It fine-tunes the model to follow instructions and behave as a useful assistant, rather than just continuing arbitrary text.
questions.hint: A raw next-token predictor doesn't naturally answer questions politely.
questions.fun_fact: ChatGPT is a fine-tuned version of the GPT base models, tuned to be an assistant.

questions.question: In fine-tuning, what does it mean to freeze layers, and why might you do it?
questions.answer: Frozen layers are kept unchanged during training, so only the remaining layers update. It saves computation and preserves lower-level features learned during pretraining.
key_points: Frozen layers don't change during backpropagation
questions.hint: It's about which parts of the network you allow to update.
questions.fun_fact: With LoRA, a model with billions of parameters can be fine-tuned using only several million extra parameters.

questions.question: In RLHF, how is the reward model built before the policy is trained?
questions.answer: Humans rank or compare model outputs, and a reward model is trained in a supervised way to predict which responses are good or bad. It then serves as the reward function for reinforcement learning.
key_points: Reward model trained by supervised learning
It scores responses as high or low reward
questions.hint: The reward isn't hand-coded; it's learned from people's judgments.
questions.fun_fact: Rankings from human annotators can be converted into scores using the Elo rating system, borrowed from ranking chess players.

questions.question: Why is human feedback a practical training signal when the task itself is hard to specify?
questions.answer: Because some tasks are hard to define explicitly but easy to judge, like whether text is helpful and harmless. Humans can swiftly compare outputs, so their judgments become the reward.
key_points: Hard to specify, easy to judge
Humans compare harmfulness or helpfulness quickly
questions.hint: Think about writing safe text versus rating it.
questions.fun_fact: RLHF gained much of its popularity when OpenAI reused it in their paper on InstructGPT.

questions.question: How does DPO differ from the classic RLHF pipeline at a high level?
questions.answer: DPO skips training a separate reward model and doing reinforcement learning, instead directly optimizing the policy on preference data. This makes preference tuning simpler and more stable than the RLHF loop.
questions.hint: It removes the middleman between human preferences and the policy update.
questions.fun_fact: RLHF reward models are typically optimized with algorithms like proximal policy optimization, the same family of methods used elsewhere in RL.

questions.question: What are the main challenges of collecting preference data for RLHF?
questions.answer: High-quality preference data is expensive to source, and if it isn't collected from a representative sample of people, the trained model can exhibit unwanted biases.
key_points: Small datasets can work but diversity matters
questions.hint: The problems come from who provides the feedback and how much it costs.
questions.fun_fact: Studies show that increasing the size of the reward model can matter more than proportionally increasing the amount of feedback data.

questions.question: Why can fine-tuning hurt a model, and what's one way to mitigate that?
questions.answer: Fine-tuning can degrade robustness to distribution shifts, hurting out-of-distribution performance. Interpolating the fine-tuned weights with the original model's weights can recover much of that robustness.
key_points: Fine-tuning reduces robustness to distribution shift
Weight interpolation with the original model
questions.hint: The fix involves blending the new model back toward its old self.
questions.fun_fact: This interpolation trick largely keeps the fine-tuned model's in-distribution performance while restoring out-of-distribution performance.

topic: How large language models are trained
